Projective symmetry groups beyond spin-1/21/2: Classifying integer-spin quantum spin liquids

Atanu Maity Affiliation: Institut für Theoretische Physik und Astrophysik and Würzburg-Dresden Cluster of Excellence ctd.qmat, Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg, Am Hubland, Campus Süd, Würzburg 97074, Germany Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India    Chunxiao Liu Affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Laboratoire de Physique des Solides, 91405 Orsay, France    Rhine Samajdar Affiliation: Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA    Yasir Iqbal Email: yiqbal@physics.iitm.ac.in Affiliation: Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Technology Madras, Chennai 600036, India
October 21, 2026
Abstract

Wen’s projective symmetry group (PSG), introduced a quarter of a century ago, reduced the classification of symmetric quantum spin liquids to an algebraic problem and has guided the study of spin-1/21/2 models and materials ever since. Many current candidate materials and quantum simulators, however, have spin-11 or larger moments, and no comparable classification exists for them. We formulate the PSG for fermionic partons of arbitrary spin SS. Integer and half-odd-integer spins already differ in their gauge structure. Half-odd-integer spins give the familiar SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} invariant gauge groups, while integer spins give a different hierarchy that includes U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} and ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}; the latter has no spin-1/21/2 counterpart. Three lattice-independent results follow for integer spin. Singlet pairing of the partons is odd under site exchange. A lattice symmetry can exchange the particle and hole representations of the local constraint, which forces symmetry-related sites into opposite constraint sectors. And a time-reversal-symmetric U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state with the same constraint on every site can be gapped only if the number of sites per unit cell is a multiple of 2​S+12S+1. We apply the formalism to the spin-11 diamond lattice, realized in frustrated A-site spinels, and find ten fully symmetric Ansätze up to second neighbors. In the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model at the mean-field level, the ground state depends on how the constraint is imposed. With the particle and hole representations, the lowest states are fully gapped U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states whose two sublattices sit in opposite constraint sectors, and one of them is gauge equivalent to a paired Ansatz. The classification provides a starting point for integer-spin quantum spin liquids on other lattices and in other materials.

I Introduction

Not every phase of matter is captured by Landau’s paradigm of spontaneous symmetry breaking. Quantum spin liquids (QSLs) [2] are the clearest example. In these magnets quantum fluctuations prevent order down to zero temperature, the excitations carry fractions of the quantum numbers of the spins, and they interact through emergent gauge fields, often with topological order [42, 40, 12]. No local order parameter tells one QSL from another, so describing them required new concepts. Wen provided them a quarter of a century ago [43]. Phases with the same symmetries can differ in how those symmetries act on the fractionalized excitations; Wen called this distinction quantum order and characterized it by the projective symmetry group (PSG).

When a spin-1/21/2 moment is written in terms of Abrikosov fermions, a microscopic symmetry need only be realized up to a gauge transformation of the partons. The PSG records how each symmetry is realized in this sense. It sorts the symmetric mean-field Ansätze into classes with emergent SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge structure and allows one to enumerate them [43]. In the twenty-five years since, this classification has become the usual way to go from a frustrated spin-1/21/2 Hamiltonian to a short list of candidate spin liquids, and from there to variational wave functions, low-energy field theories, and predictions for experiment. It has been applied to the kagome [38, 27], triangular [28, 18], and Kitaev honeycomb [44] lattices in two dimensions and to the pyrochlore [23] and diamond [10] lattices in three.

All of this work concerns spin 1/21/2, but many of the materials now studied as QSL candidates have spin 11 or larger. Several frustrated spin-11 and higher-spin magnets show strongly suppressed ordering, broad excitation continua, field-induced dynamical regimes, or behavior close to a spin liquid. Spin-11 examples include the triangular magnet NiGa2S4 [34, 26], the pyrochlore fluoride NaCaNi2F7 [37], the langbeinite K2Ni2(SO4)3 [45, 14], and diamond-lattice A-site spinels such as NiRh2O4 [9, 7]. In spin-3/23/2 and spin-5/25/2 magnets such as CoAl2O4 [30], MnSc2S4 [13], KSrFe2(PO4)3 [6], and Li9Fe3(P2O7)3(PO4)2 [20], frustration likewise suppresses or reshapes conventional order. Synthetic quantum systems offer another route. Programmable arrays of neutral atoms have been used to study frustrated quantum magnets, including a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} topological spin liquid [41, 32, 31]. The same platforms can also encode higher spins: three Rydberg levels of a single atom form an effective spin 11, which leads to dipolar spin-11 models with lattice supersolids and simplex phases on frustrated lattices [24] and to the spin-11 Haldane phase in one dimension [33]. In ultracold alkaline-earth atoms, the nuclear and electronic degrees of freedom decouple, which yields SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N)-symmetric magnets that are predicted to host spin-liquid ground states [15, 8]. In these platforms the spin can be chosen by design, so the question of which spin liquids are available to integer spins arises in quantum simulation as well as in materials.

With so many higher-spin candidates in both settings, a PSG classification for spin SS is now needed. It cannot be obtained by simply adding parton flavors. Liu, Zhou, and Ng [25, 26] introduced fermionic representations of arbitrary spin SS, in which a spin-SS moment is described by 2​S+12S+1 fermion flavors subject to a local constraint. For S>1/2S\!>\!1/2 the particle-hole equivalence of spin 1/21/2 is lost, and the internal redundancy depends on whether SS is integer or half-odd-integer: half-odd-integer spins keep an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2)-type gauge structure, whereas integer spins have a U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} structure [25]. In fermionic mean-field theory this difference underlies the even-odd effects of one-dimensional antiferromagnets. In two dimensions it allows new spin-11 spin liquids on the triangular lattice, including gapless ff-wave and chiral px+i​pyp_{x}+ip_{y} states [25, 26].

A related even-odd distinction appears in a different higher-spin parton construction. In the spin-SS Kitaev honeycomb model, the conserved plaquette operators remain exact ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge fluxes for any SS, even though the model is not integrable for SS >> 1/21/2 [29]. The corresponding ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge charges are fermions for half-odd-integer spin and bosons for integer spin. Fermionic charges must remain deconfined, while bosonic charges can condense and give a trivial paramagnet. The Kitaev construction uses Majorana partons rather than the representation used here, but it points to the same conclusion. Integer and half-odd-integer spins can differ already in their emergent gauge structure and in the nature of their fractionalized excitations.

Even so, there is still no counterpart of Wen’s classification for S>1/2S\!>\!1/2, and so no systematic way to list the symmetric spin liquids available to a higher-spin magnet. We construct this classification here for fermionic spin-SS partons. The invariant gauge groups (IGGs) depend on the parity of 2​S2S. Half-odd-integer spins give the familiar hierarchy of SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} IGGs, while integer spins give U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}, U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} IGG has no counterpart in the spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov-fermion classification and follows from the internal gauge structure of integer spins. Integer-spin QSLs can thus realize symmetries projectively in ways that spin-1/21/2 QSLs cannot.

The construction also has physical consequences that hold on any lattice. First, the singlet pairing field of integer-spin partons is odd under exchange of the two sites, whereas that of spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov fermions is even (Sec. II); integer-spin paired states use different pairing channels. Second, for S>1/2S\!>\!1/2 the particle and hole representations of the local constraint are inequivalent, and the gauge transformation that accompanies a lattice symmetry can exchange them. A symmetric state is then forced to place symmetry-related sites in opposite constraint sectors, unless it is self-dual (Appendix F). Third, a counting argument valid for any spin gives a filling constraint. An integer-spin, time-reversal-symmetric U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state with all sites in the same constraint sector can be gapped only if the number of sites per unit cell is a multiple of 2​S+12S+1 (Sec. VI). Otherwise it has a spinon Fermi surface, and a gapped symmetric spin liquid must be paired or gauge equivalent to a state with sites in opposite sectors. None of these statements requires a calculation of energies.

As a first application we take the spin-11 diamond lattice, for two reasons. One is materials. A-site spinels, with magnetic ions on the diamond lattice, form a large family of frustrated three-dimensional magnets. The nearest-neighbor diamond-lattice antiferromagnet is bipartite, but a sizable second-neighbor exchange frustrates the two interpenetrating FCC sublattices and produces a degenerate surface of spiral ground states [4]. This mechanism has been used to explain the suppressed ordering and spiral correlations of several A-site spinels with S=3/2S=3/2, 22, and 5/25/2. The spin-11 compound NiRh2O4 has motivated studies of spin-liquid behavior in spin-11 diamond antiferromagnets [9, 7]; pseudofermion functional renormalization group calculations find that the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} diamond antiferromagnet does not order for S≤1S\leq 1 in the spiral regime, which points to a quantum spiral spin liquid for spin 11 [7].

The other is gauge theory. The pyrochlore lattice is the medial lattice of the diamond lattice: pyrochlore sites sit on the bonds that connect neighboring tetrahedron centers. In quantum spin ice and related pyrochlore Coulomb phases, the spins can be viewed as variables on the links of a diamond lattice. The compact U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) gauge field lives on these links, and the electric charges, or spinons, live on the diamond-lattice sites [17, 39, 21, 3]. A PSG always refers to a particular fractional excitation, and spinon PSGs describe how symmetries act on the spin-carrying partons. Spinon PSGs on the diamond lattice thus bear on pyrochlore magnets as well.

Our main results are the following.

  1. (i)

    A PSG classification for any spin. We extend Wen’s construction to fermionic partons of arbitrary spin SS (Sec. III). The gauge group of the partons, the hierarchy of invariant gauge groups, and the procedure for solving the PSG conditions are independent of the lattice. Hopping-only Ansätze have the same link structure for integer and half-odd-integer spin, so existing spin-1/21/2 classifications can be used as the starting point for higher-spin ones.

  2. (ii)

    A new gauge-group hierarchy for integer spin. Integer spins realize the invariant gauge groups U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}, U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} (Fig. 1). The ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} spin liquids have no spin-1/21/2 counterpart.

  3. (iii)

    Lattice-independent constraints on integer-spin liquids. Odd singlet pairing, the exchange of constraint sectors by lattice symmetries, and the filling constraint on gapped U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states (Sec. VI) restrict which integer-spin liquids are possible on any lattice.

  4. (iv)

    The complete short-range classification on the spin-11 diamond lattice. Up to second-neighbor bonds there are ten fully symmetric Ansätze, two of them with a ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} IGG (Sec. IV); third-neighbor bonds add four ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants.

  5. (v)

    Energetics and experimental fingerprints. In the spin-11 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model the implementation of the local constraint decides the ground state. With the particle and hole representations, the lowest states are fully gapped U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states with the two sublattices in opposite constraint sectors, one of them gauge equivalent to a paired Ansatz (Sec. V). We give their static structure factors, the quantities measured by neutron scattering, and compare them with the classical spiral surface (Sec. VII).

The paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the fermionic representation of a spin-SS moment and the corresponding mean-field theory. Section III develops the PSG construction for spin-SS partons and the IGG hierarchies for integer and half-odd-integer spin. Section IV applies it to the spin-11 diamond lattice and lists the fully symmetric short-range Ansätze. Section V studies the spin-11 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model within these Ansätze, for the particle, hole, and particle-hole-symmetric implementations of the constraint and for the particle-hole-averaged representation of Ref. [25]. Section VI derives a filling constraint on gapped U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states for general SS, and Sec. VII discusses the static structure factors of the lowest states and compares them with the classical Luttinger-Tisza analysis. Section VIII summarizes the results.

II Fermionic spin-SS representation and mean-field construction

We first recall the fermionic representation of a spin-SS moment introduced in Ref. [25]. Each site carries 2​S+12S+1 fermion flavors fmf_{m}, m=−S,−S+1,…,Sm=-S,-S+1,\ldots,S, and

Sα=fm†​Σm​nα​fn,S^{\alpha}=f_{m}^{\dagger}\Sigma^{\alpha}_{mn}f_{n}, (1)

where repeated flavor indices are summed and Σα\Sigma^{\alpha} (α=x,y,z\alpha=x,y,z) are the spin-SS matrices. The local Hilbert space is enlarged from the (2​S+1)(2S+1)-dimensional spin space to a fermionic Fock space of dimension 22​S+12^{2S+1}. There are two ways to recover the physical space, which look alike but are, in general, different. The particle representation imposes single occupancy,

Nf=∑m=−SSfm†​fm=1,N_{f}=\sum_{m=-S}^{S}f_{m}^{\dagger}f_{m}=1, (2)

and the hole representation imposes

Nf=2​S,N_{f}=2S, (3)

i.e., a single hole among the 2​S+12S+1 flavors. The two constraints coincide only for S=1/2S=1/2, so the particle-hole equivalence of the spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov-fermion construction is lost for S>1/2S>1/2 [25].

As in the spin-1/21/2 construction of Ref. [1], we combine the fermions into the two-column object

ψ=(F,F¯),\psi=(F,\bar{F}), (4)

where

F=(fS,fS−1,…,f−S)T,F=\left(f_{S},f_{S-1},\ldots,f_{-S}\right)^{\mathrm{T}}, (5)

and

F¯=(f−S†,−f−S+1†,…,(−1)2​S​fS†)T.\bar{F}=\big(f^{\dagger}_{-S},-f^{\dagger}_{-S+1},\ldots,(-1)^{2S}f^{\dagger}_{S}\big)^{\mathrm{T}}. (6)

The spin operator then reads

Sα=12​Tr​[ψ†​Σα​ψ],S^{\alpha}=\frac{1}{2}{\rm Tr}\!\left[\psi^{\dagger}\Sigma^{\alpha}\psi\right], (7)

where Σα\Sigma^{\alpha} are the (2​S+1)×(2​S+1)(2S+1)\times(2S+1) spin-SS generators of SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), and the trace is over the two-column internal space. In this form the internal redundancy of the representation is easy to see. The spin operator is unchanged under a right multiplication

ψi→ψi​Wi,\psi_{i}\rightarrow\psi_{i}W_{i}, (8)

which suggests a U⁡(2)\mathrm{U}(2) gauge freedom acting on the two columns of ψi\psi_{i}. The two columns FiF_{i} and F¯i\bar{F}_{i} are, however, not independent spinors, and only transformations that preserve the canonical anticommutation relations are allowed. The resulting internal symmetry group is

ISG={SU⁡(2),S∈ℤ+12,U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2,S∈ℤ.{\rm ISG}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{SU}(2),&S\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2},\\ \mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2},&S\in\mathbb{Z}.\end{cases} (9)

The internal structure of the representation thus differs between half-odd-integer and integer spins, and this difference runs through the whole spin-SS PSG classification.

The mean-field theory is built from spin-rotation-invariant link variables. A physical spin rotation acts from the left,

ψi→G​ψi,\psi_{i}\rightarrow G\psi_{i}, (10)

where GG is the (2​S+1)(2S+1)-dimensional irreducible representation of an SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) spin rotation, so the bilinear

U^i​j=ψi†​ψj\hat{U}_{ij}=\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\psi_{j} (11)

is a spin singlet. It is a 2×22\times 2 matrix in the internal space of ψ\psi and serves as the link variable on the bond i​jij. In terms of FF and F¯\bar{F} it contains the singlet hopping and pairing fields

χ^i​j=Fi†​Fj,η^i​j=F¯i†​Fj,\hat{\chi}_{ij}=F_{i}^{\dagger}F_{j},\qquad\hat{\eta}_{ij}=\bar{F}_{i}^{\dagger}F_{j}, (12)

and takes the form

U^i​j=(χ^i​j(−1)2​S+1​η^i​j†η^i​j−χ^i​j†).\hat{U}_{ij}=\begin{pmatrix}\hat{\chi}_{ij}&(-1)^{2S+1}\hat{\eta}^{\dagger}_{ij}\\ \hat{\eta}_{ij}&-\hat{\chi}^{\dagger}_{ij}\end{pmatrix}. (13)

Under exchange of the two sites,

χ^j​i=χ^i​j†,η^j​i=(−1)2​S+1​η^i​j.\hat{\chi}_{ji}=\hat{\chi}^{\dagger}_{ij},\qquad\hat{\eta}_{ji}=(-1)^{2S+1}\hat{\eta}_{ij}. (14)

so the singlet pairing field is odd under site interchange for integer spin and even for half-odd-integer spin.

The local constraints are also simple in this notation. For integer spin, the particle and hole representations read

Tr⁡[ψi​τ3​ψi†]\displaystyle{\rm Tr}\!\left[\psi_{i}\tau^{3}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right] =ζ⁡(2​S−1),\displaystyle=\zeta(2S-1),
ζ\displaystyle\zeta ={+1,Nf=1,−1,Nf=2​S,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}+1,&N_{f}=1,\\ -1,&N_{f}=2S,\end{cases} (15)

where the Pauli matrix τ3\tau^{3} acts in the internal space of ψ\psi. The U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) part of U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} preserves the choice of ζ\zeta, while the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} part exchanges the particle and hole representations. For a fixed representation, one Lagrange multiplier λi\lambda_{i} per site is enough to impose the constraint.

Three groups should be kept apart. (i) U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} is the internal symmetry of the spin operator, i.e., of the unconstrained representation. (ii) Once an embedding, ζ=+1\zeta=+1 or ζ=−1\zeta=-1, is chosen on every site, only the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) subgroup preserves the constraint; the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} coset maps the particle theory onto the hole theory. (iii) In the particle-hole-averaged (or projected) formulation of Ref. [25], which treats both embeddings alike, the full group acts as a gauge symmetry. The PSG classification below takes the gauge transformations from the full group, which is appropriate for the link sector and for the particle-hole-symmetric saddle point. At fixed integer filling, an Ansatz whose PSG contains ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}-coset elements is symmetric only if the constraint label is transformed along with it, i.e., if sites related by such an element carry opposite embeddings. Section V works out what this means for the phase diagram.

For half-odd-integer spin the internal symmetry is SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), and the constraint is a vector in the internal space,

Tr⁡[ψi​𝝉​ψi†]=(0,0,ζ⁡(2​S−1)),{\rm Tr}\!\left[\psi_{i}\bm{\tau}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right]=\bigl(0,0,\zeta(2S-1)\bigr), (16)

where 𝝉=(τ1,τ2,τ3)\bm{\tau}=(\tau^{1},\tau^{2},\tau^{3}) acts in the two-column internal space of ψ\psi, and ζ=+1\zeta=+1 (−1-1) corresponds to the particle (hole) representation. An internal SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) rotation changes the direction of this vector, so three Lagrange multipliers 𝝀i=(λi1,λi2,λi3)\bm{\lambda}_{i}=(\lambda_{i}^{1},\lambda_{i}^{2},\lambda_{i}^{3}) are needed, as in the spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov-fermion formulation.

At the mean-field level we decouple the spin-rotation-invariant channel with the cc-number link variable

ui​j=⟨U^i​j⟩.u_{ij}=\langle\hat{U}_{ij}\rangle. (17)

The quadratic Hamiltonian is

H^MF=\displaystyle\hat{H}_{\rm MF}= a⁡(S)2∑i​jJi​j{Tr(ui​j†ui​j)\displaystyle\;\frac{a(S)}{2}\sum_{ij}J_{ij}\Bigg\{{\rm Tr}\!\left(u_{ij}^{\dagger}u_{ij}\right)
−Tr[ui​j†ψi†ψj+H.c.]}+H^c,\displaystyle\qquad-{\rm Tr}\!\left[u_{ij}^{\dagger}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\psi_{j}+{\rm H.c.}\right]\Bigg\}+\hat{H}_{c}, (18)

where a⁡(S)a(S) is a spin-dependent coefficient, the sum runs over ordered pairs (i,j)(i,j), so that each bond is counted twice, and the trace is over the internal indices. For S=1S=1 the Heisenberg exchange can be written exactly as J​𝐒i⋅𝐒j=−J:(χ^i​j†​χ^i​j+η^i​j†​η^i​j):J\,\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}=-J:\!(\hat{\chi}^{\dagger}_{ij}\hat{\chi}_{ij}+\hat{\eta}^{\dagger}_{ij}\hat{\eta}_{ij})\!: [25]. Equation (18) with a⁡(1)=1/2a(1)=1/2 is then the complete mean-field decoupling of the Heisenberg model. For S>1S>1 the exchange also contains triplet and higher-multipole channels [25], and Eq. (18) is a spin-rotation-invariant trial Hamiltonian in the singlet channel only. For integer spin the constraint term is

H^c=∑iλi​[Tr⁡(ψi​τ3​ψi†)−ζ⁡(2​S−1)],\hat{H}_{c}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\left[{\rm Tr}\!\left(\psi_{i}\tau^{3}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right)-\zeta(2S-1)\right], (19)

and for half-odd-integer spin

H^c=∑i𝝀i⋅[Tr⁡(ψi​𝝉​ψi†)−(0,0,ζ⁡(2​S−1))].\hat{H}_{c}=\sum_{i}\bm{\lambda}_{i}\cdot\left[{\rm Tr}\!\left(\psi_{i}\bm{\tau}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right)-\bigl(0,0,\zeta(2S-1)\bigr)\right]. (20)

Here ζ=+1\zeta=+1 and −1-1 denote the particle and hole representations.

The redundancy of the representation acts as a local gauge transformation. Under

ψi→ψi​Wi,Wi∈ISG,\psi_{i}\rightarrow\psi_{i}W_{i},\qquad W_{i}\in{\rm ISG}, (21)

the mean-field link and constraint fields transform as

ui​j→Wi†​ui​j​Wj.u_{ij}\rightarrow W_{i}^{\dagger}u_{ij}W_{j}. (22)

For integer spin,

λi​τ3→Wi†​λi​τ3​Wi,\lambda_{i}\tau^{3}\rightarrow W_{i}^{\dagger}\lambda_{i}\tau^{3}W_{i}, (23)

whereas for half-odd-integer spin,

𝝀i⋅𝝉→Wi†​(𝝀i⋅𝝉)​Wi.\bm{\lambda}_{i}\cdot\bm{\tau}\rightarrow W_{i}^{\dagger}\big(\bm{\lambda}_{i}\cdot\bm{\tau}\big)W_{i}. (24)

Equation (18) is invariant under these transformations. This is the starting point of the PSG construction: a physical symmetry need not leave an Ansatz invariant by itself, as long as it does so when combined with a gauge transformation.

III Projective symmetry group for spin-SS partons

At the saddle point the operator-valued link field is replaced by its expectation value, ui​j=⟨U^i​j⟩u_{ij}=\langle\hat{U}_{ij}\rangle, and the onsite constraint is imposed only on average through a Lagrange multiplier field. We write the corresponding matrix in the internal space as

Λi={λi​τ3,S∈ℤ,𝝀i⋅𝝉,S∈ℤ+12,\Lambda_{i}=\begin{cases}\lambda_{i}\tau^{3},&S\in\mathbb{Z},\\ \bm{\lambda}_{i}\cdot\bm{\tau},&S\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2},\end{cases} (25)

where 𝝉=(τ1,τ2,τ3)\bm{\tau}=(\tau^{1},\tau^{2},\tau^{3}) acts on the two columns of ψ\psi. A mean-field Ansatz is specified by the set

𝒜={ui​j,Λi}.\mathcal{A}=\{u_{ij},\Lambda_{i}\}. (26)

Ansätze related by a local ISG transformation describe the same physical spin state before projection. This local ISG redundancy is why symmetries can be realized projectively.

Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} be a symmetry of the lattice space group, with the convention that site ii is mapped to 𝒪⁡(i)\mathcal{O}(i). Acting with 𝒪\mathcal{O} alone sends the Ansatz to

𝒪:{ui​j,Λi}⟶{u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j),Λ𝒪⁡(i)}.\mathcal{O}:\{u_{ij},\Lambda_{i}\}\longrightarrow\{u_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)},\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}(i)}\}. (27)

The Ansatz is symmetric under 𝒪\mathcal{O} if the transformed Ansatz is gauge-equivalent to the original one, i.e., if there is a site-dependent internal transformation W𝒪W_{\mathcal{O}} such that

W𝒪†​[𝒪⁡(i)]​u𝒪⁡(i)​𝒪​(j)​W𝒪​[𝒪⁡(j)]\displaystyle W_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}[\mathcal{O}(i)]\,u_{\mathcal{O}(i)\mathcal{O}(j)}\,W_{\mathcal{O}}[\mathcal{O}(j)] =ui​j,\displaystyle=u_{ij}, (28)
W𝒪†​[𝒪⁡(i)]​Λ𝒪⁡(i)​W𝒪​[𝒪⁡(i)]\displaystyle W_{\mathcal{O}}^{\dagger}[\mathcal{O}(i)]\,\Lambda_{\mathcal{O}(i)}\,W_{\mathcal{O}}[\mathcal{O}(i)] =Λi.\displaystyle=\Lambda_{i}.

The pair (𝒪,W𝒪)(\mathcal{O},W_{\mathcal{O}}) is then an element of the projective symmetry group. A physical symmetry thus need not act linearly on the partons; it may come with a gauge transformation in the internal space.

Time reversal is antiunitary and needs separate treatment. We write

𝒯=𝒰𝒯​𝒦,𝒰𝒯=e−i​π​Sy,\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{K},\qquad\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}=e^{-i\pi S^{y}}, (29)

where 𝒦\mathcal{K} denotes complex conjugation. The spin matrices obey

𝒯​Siα​𝒯−1=−Siα.\mathcal{T}S_{i}^{\alpha}\mathcal{T}^{-1}=-S_{i}^{\alpha}. (30)

On the two-column fermion field, time reversal acts as

ψi→𝒰𝒯​𝒦​ψi.\psi_{i}\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{K}\psi_{i}. (31)

In a projective implementation this operation may be followed by an internal transformation,

ψi→𝒰𝒯​𝒦​ψi​W𝒯​(i).\psi_{i}\rightarrow\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{K}\psi_{i}\,W_{\mathcal{T}}(i). (32)

To obtain the condition on the link matrix, consider the bilinear

Tr⁡(ψi​ui​j​ψj†).{\rm Tr}\!\left(\psi_{i}u_{ij}\psi_{j}^{\dagger}\right). (33)

Under projective time reversal it transforms as

Tr⁡(ψi​ui​j​ψj†)→Tr⁡[𝒰𝒯​ψi​W𝒯∗​(i)​ui​j∗​W𝒯T​(j)​ψj†​𝒰𝒯†].\begin{split}{\rm Tr}\!\left(\psi_{i}u_{ij}\psi_{j}^{\dagger}\right)\rightarrow{\rm Tr}\!\left[\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}\psi_{i}W_{\mathcal{T}}^{\ast}(i)u_{ij}^{\ast}W_{\mathcal{T}}^{T}(j)\psi_{j}^{\dagger}\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}\right].\end{split} (34)

The complex conjugation of the gauge matrix can be removed using

W∗=τν​W​τν,ν={1,S∈ℤ,2,S∈ℤ+12,W^{\ast}=\tau^{\nu}W\tau^{\nu},\qquad\nu=\begin{cases}1,&S\in\mathbb{Z},\\ 2,&S\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2},\end{cases} (35)

with W∈U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2W\in\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} for integer spin and W∈SU⁡(2)W\in\mathrm{SU}(2) for half-odd-integer spin. A spin-rotation-invariant link matrix can be written as

ui​j=i​λi​j0​τ0+λi​j3​τ3+ip​λi​j1​τ1+ip​λi​j2​τ2,u_{ij}=i\lambda_{ij}^{0}\tau^{0}+\lambda_{ij}^{3}\tau^{3}+i^{p}\lambda_{ij}^{1}\tau^{1}+i^{p}\lambda_{ij}^{2}\tau^{2}, (36)

where p=(2​S+1)mod2p=(2S+1)\bmod 2 and all λi​jγ\lambda_{ij}^{\gamma} are real. The τ0\tau^{0} and τ3\tau^{3} components are singlet hopping amplitudes and the τ1\tau^{1} and τ2\tau^{2} components are singlet pairing amplitudes; in the canonical Ansätze of the appendices, these are denoted χi​j0=λi​j0\chi^{0}_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}^{0}, χi​j3=λi​j3\chi^{3}_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}^{3}, Δi​j1=λi​j1\Delta^{1}_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}^{1}, and Δi​j2=λi​j2\Delta^{2}_{ij}=\lambda_{ij}^{2}. With this convention,

τν​ui​j∗​τν=−ui​j.\tau^{\nu}u_{ij}^{\ast}\tau^{\nu}=-u_{ij}. (37)

Using also WT=(W∗)†=τν​W†​τνW^{T}=(W^{\ast})^{\dagger}=\tau^{\nu}W^{\dagger}\tau^{\nu}, the transformed bilinear becomes −Tr⁡[𝒰𝒯​ψi​(τν​W𝒯​(i))​ui​j​(τν​W𝒯​(j))†​ψj†​𝒰𝒯†]-{\rm Tr}[\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}\psi_{i}\,(\tau^{\nu}W_{\mathcal{T}}(i))\,u_{ij}\,(\tau^{\nu}W_{\mathcal{T}}(j))^{\dagger}\psi_{j}^{\dagger}\mathcal{U}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}]. We absorb the extra τν\tau^{\nu} into the gauge part of time reversal by defining

W~𝒯​(i)={[τ1​W𝒯​(i)]†=W𝒯†​(i)​τ1,S∈ℤ,[i​τ2​W𝒯​(i)]†=−i​W𝒯†​(i)​τ2,S∈ℤ+12.\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}}(i)=\begin{cases}\big[\tau^{1}W_{\mathcal{T}}(i)\big]^{\dagger}=W^{\dagger}_{\mathcal{T}}(i)\tau^{1},&S\in\mathbb{Z},\\ \big[i\tau^{2}W_{\mathcal{T}}(i)\big]^{\dagger}=-iW^{\dagger}_{\mathcal{T}}(i)\tau^{2},&S\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{cases} (38)

With this gauge matrix the time-reversal condition on the Ansatz reads

W~𝒯†​(i)​ui​j​W~𝒯​(j)\displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}(i)\,u_{ij}\,\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}}(j) =−ui​j,\displaystyle=-u_{ij}, (39)
W~𝒯†​(i)​Λi​W~𝒯​(i)\displaystyle\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}}^{\dagger}(i)\,\Lambda_{i}\,\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}}(i) =−Λi.\displaystyle=-\Lambda_{i}.

The minus sign comes from the antiunitarity of time reversal together with our convention for the singlet link variable. Equation (39) is the time-reversal analog of the unitary PSG condition in Eq. (28). In the appendices the gauge part of time reversal is written as W𝒯​(r,μ)W_{\mathcal{T}}(r,\mu); it is the matrix W~𝒯\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}} of Eq. (39), so that all PSG conditions involving 𝒯\mathcal{T} are imposed on W~𝒯\widetilde{W}_{\mathcal{T}} with the minus sign of Eq. (39).

The invariant gauge group (IGG) is the group of pure gauge transformations that leave the Ansatz unchanged, i.e., the PSG elements whose physical part is the identity. An element 𝒲i∈IGG\mathcal{W}_{i}\in{\rm IGG} satisfies

𝒲i†​ui​j​𝒲j\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{i}^{\dagger}u_{ij}\mathcal{W}_{j} =ui​j,\displaystyle=u_{ij}, (40)
𝒲i†​Λi​𝒲i\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{i}^{\dagger}\Lambda_{i}\mathcal{W}_{i} =Λi.\displaystyle=\Lambda_{i}.

The IGG is the kernel of the projection of the PSG onto the physical symmetry group. Equivalently, algebraic relations among the physical symmetries need to hold only up to elements of the IGG. Since Λi\Lambda_{i} is part of the Ansatz and τ1​Λi​τ1=−Λi\tau^{1}\Lambda_{i}\tau^{1}=-\Lambda_{i}, a nonzero onsite field removes the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} coset from the IGG of the link sector, U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2→U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}\to\mathrm{U}(1) and ℤ2×ℤ2→ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}\to\mathbb{Z}_{2}; the IGGs quoted in the classification below refer to the link sector.

The IGG is determined by which link components an Ansatz contains. In a canonical gauge the IGG is a subgroup of the global internal symmetry group; the canonical forms are shown in Fig. 1. For half-odd-integer spin the possible IGGs are

SU⁡(2),U⁡(1),ℤ2,\mathrm{SU}(2),\qquad\mathrm{U}(1),\qquad\mathbb{Z}_{2}, (41)

with representative global gauge matrices

{ei​ϕ​𝐧^⋅𝝉},{ei​ϕ​τ3},{±τ0},\left\{e^{i\phi\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}\cdot\bm{\tau}}\right\},\qquad\left\{e^{i\phi\tau^{3}}\right\},\qquad\left\{\pm\tau^{0}\right\}, (42)

respectively. For integer spin, the corresponding possibilities are

U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2,U⁡(1),ℤ2,ℤ2×ℤ2,\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2},\qquad\mathrm{U}(1),\qquad\mathbb{Z}_{2},\qquad\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, (43)

with canonical representatives

{ei​ϕ​τ3,ei​ϕ​τ3​τ1},{ei​ϕ​τ3},\displaystyle\left\{e^{i\phi\tau^{3}},\,e^{i\phi\tau^{3}}\tau^{1}\right\},\qquad\left\{e^{i\phi\tau^{3}}\right\}, (44)
{±τ0},{±τ0,±τ1}.\displaystyle\left\{\pm\tau^{0}\right\},\qquad\left\{\pm\tau^{0},\,\pm\tau^{1}\right\}.

Here, ϕ\phi is a real parameter, 𝐧^\hat{\mathbf{n}} is a unit vector in the internal SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) space, and τ0\tau^{0} is the 2×22\times 2 identity matrix. The first integer-spin group is the orthogonal group O⁡(2)≃U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2O(2)\simeq\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}: the element τ1\tau^{1} acts on the continuous subgroup by inversion, τ1​ei​ϕ​τ3​τ1=e−i​ϕ​τ3\tau^{1}e^{i\phi\tau^{3}}\tau^{1}=e^{-i\phi\tau^{3}}, so the product is semidirect rather than direct. The last group is the Klein four-group.

The exchange property of the hopping field has a simple consequence. Since χj​i=χi​j†\chi_{ji}=\chi_{ij}^{\dagger} for both integer and half-odd-integer spins, hopping-only Ansätze have the same link structure in the two cases. Their IGGs can still differ, because the allowed gauge transformations differ. For example, the canonical Ansatz with only the λi​j0\lambda_{ij}^{0} component nonzero has IGG U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} for integer spin, whereas the corresponding half-odd-integer Ansatz has IGG SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2), as shown in Fig. 1. Integer and half-odd-integer spins thus differ both in the parity of the pairing field and in the group of allowed gauge transformations.

For an Ansatz that is not in the canonical gauge, the IGG is most easily found from gauge-covariant flux operators. Let 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j} be a closed loop based at site jj and passing through the ordered sequence of sites

𝒞j=(j,k,l,…,m,j).\mathcal{C}_{j}=(j,k,l,\ldots,m,j). (45)

The flux operator is

P𝒞j=P(j,k,l,…,m,j)=uj​kuk​l⋯um​j.P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}=P(j,k,l,\ldots,m,j)=u_{jk}u_{kl}\cdots u_{mj}. (46)

Under a local gauge transformation ui​j→Wi†​ui​j​Wju_{ij}\rightarrow W_{i}^{\dagger}u_{ij}W_{j}, this object transforms only at the base point,

P𝒞j→Wj†​P𝒞j​Wj.P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}\rightarrow W_{j}^{\dagger}P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}W_{j}. (47)

The eigenvalues of P𝒞jP_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}, or its conjugacy class, are therefore gauge invariant. A pure gauge transformation 𝒲j\mathcal{W}_{j} belongs to the IGG only if it commutes with all flux operators based at jj,

[𝒲j,P𝒞j]=0\left[\mathcal{W}_{j},P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}\right]=0 (48)

for every closed loop 𝒞j\mathcal{C}_{j}.

In a canonical gauge the flux operator around a qq-sided loop has the form

P𝒞jint\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}^{\rm int} ∝(τ3)q​(ρ​ei​ϕ𝒞0​τ3+ρ′​ei​ϕ𝒞1​τ3​τ1),\displaystyle\propto(\tau^{3})^{q}\left(\rho\,e^{i\phi_{\mathcal{C}}^{0}\tau^{3}}+\rho^{\prime}\,e^{i\phi_{\mathcal{C}}^{1}\tau^{3}}\tau^{1}\right), (49)
P𝒞jhalf\displaystyle P_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}^{\rm half} ∝Wj​ei​ϕ𝒞​τ3​(τ3)q​Wj†,Wj∈SU⁡(2),\displaystyle\propto W_{j}e^{i\phi_{\mathcal{C}}\tau^{3}}(\tau^{3})^{q}W_{j}^{\dagger},\qquad W_{j}\in\mathrm{SU}(2), (50)

where P𝒞jintP_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}^{\rm int} and P𝒞jhalfP_{\mathcal{C}_{j}}^{\rm half} refer to the integer-spin and half-odd-integer spin cases, respectively. The phases ϕ𝒞0\phi_{\mathcal{C}}^{0}, ϕ𝒞1\phi_{\mathcal{C}}^{1}, and ϕ𝒞\phi_{\mathcal{C}} are the gauge fluxes, or Aharonov–Bohm phases, accumulated by the fermionic spinons around the loop 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For integer spin there are two U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) phases, one for each of the components τ0\tau^{0} and τ1\tau^{1} of the discrete ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} sector. Only ϕ𝒞0\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{C}}, the moduli ρ,ρ′\rho,\rho^{\prime}, and differences of ϕ1\phi^{1} between loops sharing a base point are gauge invariant: under a base-point rotation ei​θ​τ3e^{i\theta\tau^{3}} the τ1\tau^{1}-sector angle shifts, e−i​θ​τ3​(ei​ϕ1​τ3​τ1)​ei​θ​τ3=ei⁡(ϕ1−2​θ)​τ3​τ1e^{-i\theta\tau^{3}}\big(e^{i\phi^{1}\tau^{3}}\tau^{1}\big)e^{i\theta\tau^{3}}=e^{i(\phi^{1}-2\theta)\tau^{3}}\tau^{1}, so the values of ϕ1\phi^{1} quoted below are representatives in the canonical gauge of the appendices. For half-odd-integer spin there is a single SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) flux phase, up to conjugation by WjW_{j}.

IV Spin-11 PSG classification on the diamond lattice

We now classify the fully symmetric spin-11 mean-field Ansätze on the diamond lattice, using the lattice conventions and notation of Ref. [10]. The diamond lattice [Fig. 2(a)] has space group F​d​3¯​mFd\bar{3}m (No. 227). In the coordinates of Ref. [10] it is generated by the translations TiT_{i}, i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, along the three FCC primitive directions, the screw rotation S4S_{4}, and the sixfold rotoinversion C¯3\bar{C}_{3}. A fully symmetric Ansatz must also preserve time reversal 𝒯\mathcal{T} projectively.

We keep amplitudes on first- and second-neighbor bonds only. The classification then gives ten distinct symmetric Ansätze, listed in Table 1. The first seven are hopping-only Ansätze. Their link structure is the same as in the spin-1/21/2 diamond-lattice classification, because the hopping field satisfies χj​i=χi​j†\chi_{ji}=\chi_{ij}^{\dagger} for both integer and half-odd-integer spins. Their IGGs differ, however, because the internal symmetry group of the spin-11 representation differs from that of spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov fermions. The two link patterns that give SU⁡(2)\mathrm{SU}(2) Ansätze for spin 1/21/2 reappear for spin 11 with IGG U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} (first two rows of Table 1). The U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) hopping Ansätze of spin 1/21/2 also have integer-spin counterparts; with amplitudes up to second neighbors, the seven U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) Ansätze of Ref. [10] reduce to the five in rows three to seven.

The two classifications differ most once singlet pairing is allowed. For spin 11 the singlet pairing field is odd under site interchange, while for spin 1/21/2 it is even, and this changes which paired Ansätze are allowed. The spin-1/21/2 diamond-lattice classification has eight short-range ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze. For spin 11, with amplitudes up to second neighbors, only one algebraic ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG admits a nonvanishing Ansatz, ZA3110 (last row of Table 1); its derivation is given in Appendix C. Its self-consistent saddle point has χ1=0\chi_{1}=0 (Sec. V), where the IGG is enlarged to U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), so a genuine ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state requires longer-range amplitudes.

In addition, integer-spin systems permit an IGG of the form ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, which has no analog in the usual spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov-fermion PSG classification. This case is obtained by allowing only the λi​j0\lambda^{0}_{ij} and λi​j1\lambda^{1}_{ij} components of the link matrix to be nonzero, thereby breaking the continuous U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) part of the U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} structure down to a discrete subgroup. The corresponding PSG solutions are given in Appendix D; they yield two Ansätze, labeled ZZA30\mathrm{ZZA30} and ZZB10\mathrm{ZZB10}, which appear in rows eight and nine of Table 1.

We characterize the Ansätze by their gauge fluxes. Without third-neighbor amplitudes, the loop operators that involve third-neighbor bonds,

P3​t0​(ϕ3​t0),P3​t1​(ϕ3​t1),P3​r​(ϕ3​r),P_{3t_{0}}(\phi_{3t_{0}}),\qquad P_{3t_{1}}(\phi_{3t_{1}}),\qquad P_{3r}(\phi_{3r}), (51)

are not defined, and we need only the hexagonal loop Ph​(ϕh)P_{h}(\phi_{h}) and the two triangular loops Pt0​(ϕt0)P_{t_{0}}(\phi_{t_{0}}) and Pt1​(ϕt1)P_{t_{1}}(\phi_{t_{1}}), defined as in Ref. [10] and shown in Fig. 2(b). The Ansätze are then characterized by the three fluxes

(ϕh,ϕt0,ϕt1).(\phi_{h},\phi_{t_{0}},\phi_{t_{1}}). (52)

For integer spin, however, each loop flux has two components, as described in Eq. (49). We denote the flux through a loop 𝒞\mathcal{C} by

ϕ𝒞=(ϕ𝒞0,ϕ𝒞1),\phi_{\mathcal{C}}=\left(\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{C}},\phi^{1}_{\mathcal{C}}\right), (53)

where the two components are associated with the τ0\tau^{0} and τ1\tau^{1} sectors of the integer-spin flux operator. For hopping-only states, including the U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} and U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) Ansätze, the coefficient of the τ1\tau^{1} sector in Eq. (49) vanishes, ρ′=0\rho^{\prime}=0. Hence, each loop carries only the ordinary U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) flux component ϕ𝒞0\phi^{0}_{\mathcal{C}}. The flux structures of these hopping-only states are thus the same as in the corresponding spin-1/21/2 classification of Ref. [10].

For paired integer-spin Ansätze with ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} or ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} IGG, both components of the flux must be kept. We write ∗* for a sector that is absent (ρ=0\rho=0 or ρ′=0\rho^{\prime}=0 in Eq. (49)), which is different from a phase equal to zero. For the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz ZA3110\mathrm{ZA3110} with the uniform bond pattern of Table 1 and χ1​Δ1​χ2≠0\chi_{1}\Delta_{1}\chi_{2}\neq 0, the loop products give u1​u1†=(χ12+Δ12)​τ0+2​χ1​Δ1​τ2u_{1}u_{1}^{\dagger}=(\chi^{2}_{1}+\Delta^{2}_{1})\tau^{0}+2\chi_{1}\Delta_{1}\tau^{2} and u1​τ3​u1†=(χ12−Δ12)​τ3u_{1}\tau^{3}u_{1}^{\dagger}=(\chi^{2}_{1}-\Delta^{2}_{1})\tau^{3}, and hence

(ϕh0,ϕh1)\displaystyle(\phi^{0}_{h},\phi^{1}_{h}) =(0,−π2),\displaystyle=\left(0,-\frac{\pi}{2}\right),
(ϕt00,ϕt01)\displaystyle(\phi^{0}_{t_{0}},\phi^{1}_{t_{0}}) =(0,−π2),\displaystyle=\left(0,-\frac{\pi}{2}\right),
(ϕt10,ϕt11)\displaystyle(\phi^{0}_{t_{1}},\phi^{1}_{t_{1}}) =(0,∗).\displaystyle=(0,*). (54)

At its self-consistent point χ1=0\chi_{1}=0 (Sec. V.4) all τ1\tau^{1} sectors vanish and the fluxes reduce to (ϕh0,ϕt00,ϕt10)=(0,0,π)(\phi^{0}_{h},\phi^{0}_{t_{0}},\phi^{0}_{t_{1}})=(0,0,\pi), the flux pattern of UA31, consistent with the gauge equivalence discussed there. As noted after Eq. (50), the values of ϕ1\phi^{1} are representatives in the canonical gauge. The two ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze, ZZA30 and ZZB10, have no second-neighbor amplitudes, so their triangular fluxes are not defined and they are characterized by the hexagonal flux alone:

ZZA30:(ϕh0,ϕh1)\displaystyle\mathrm{ZZA30}:\qquad(\phi^{0}_{h},\phi^{1}_{h}) =(0,−π2),\displaystyle=\left(0,-\frac{\pi}{2}\right), (55)
ZZB10:(ϕh0,ϕh1)\displaystyle\mathrm{ZZB10}:\qquad(\phi^{0}_{h},\phi^{1}_{h}) =(π,π2).\displaystyle=\left(\pi,\frac{\pi}{2}\right). (56)

V Mean-field phase diagram of the spin-11 J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} model

We now turn to the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model on the spin-11 diamond lattice,

H=J1​∑⟨i​j⟩1𝐒i⋅𝐒j+J2​∑⟨i​j⟩2𝐒i⋅𝐒j,H=J_{1}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{1}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}+J_{2}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_{2}}\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}, (57)

where ⟨i​j⟩1\langle ij\rangle_{1} and ⟨i​j⟩2\langle ij\rangle_{2} denote first- and second-neighbor bonds. Previous work on this model found a broad nonmagnetic regime for sizable J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} [7]. We treat it within the zeroth-order fermionic mean-field theory of Sec. II.

The classical model is well understood. The nearest-neighbor ordered state becomes unstable at J2/|J1|=1/8J_{2}/|J_{1}|=1/8, and beyond this point the ground states form a two-dimensional spiral surface in momentum space [4]. Thermal and quantum fluctuations select particular spirals from this surface by order by disorder [4, 5, 11], and finite-spin corrections can enlarge nearby collinear regions and stabilize further ordered states near special points of the surface [35, 19]. We ask a complementary question: which fully symmetric fractionalized Ansätze, among those allowed by the spin-11 gauge structure, have the lowest energy in the same frustrated regime?

For spin 11 the strict particle and hole constraints are

Tr⁡[ψi​τ3​ψi†]=±1,{\rm Tr}\!\left[\psi_{i}\tau^{3}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right]=\pm 1, (58)

with ++ for the particle (Nf=1N_{f}=1) and −- for the hole (Nf=2N_{f}=2) representation. At the saddle-point level we also consider the particle-hole-symmetric implementation,

⟨Tr⁡[ψi​τ3​ψi†]⟩=0,\left\langle{\rm Tr}\!\left[\psi_{i}\tau^{3}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}\right]\right\rangle=0, (59)

which corresponds to an average filling ⟨Nf⟩=3/2\langle N_{f}\rangle=3/2. This is a mean-field treatment of the constraint, not a projection onto either the particle or the hole Hilbert space. For S=1S=1 the exchange decouples exactly into the singlet hopping and pairing channels [25], which fixes a⁡(1)=1/2a(1)=1/2 in Eq. (18); the resulting quadratic Hamiltonian is Eq. (119) of Appendix E.

We solve the self-consistency equations for the Ansätze of Table 1 that carry second-neighbor amplitudes (UA01, UA31, UB01, UB31, and ZA3110) and compare their energies per site, E/N=⟨H^MF0⟩/NE/N=\langle\hat{H}^{0}_{\rm MF}\rangle/N, as functions of J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. At the self-consistent point this equals ⟨H⟩\langle H\rangle in the mean-field state. SA3 and SB1 are the χ2=λ=0\chi_{2}=\lambda=0 limits of UA and UB class respectively and appear in their scans. UC20, ZZA30, and ZZB10 have first-neighbor amplitudes only, so their energies do not depend on J2J_{2}; we have not computed them. Since such a state could still be lowest over a range of small J2J_{2}, “lowest state” below always refers to the five families with second-neighbor amplitudes together with SA3 and SB1.

Two features of the integer-spin gauge structure matter for a correct comparison. The first concerns UA31 and UB31, whose symmetry-allowed onsite term is staggered, Λi=±λ​τ3\Lambda_{i}=\pm\lambda\tau^{3}. This term must be determined self-consistently. The Bloch Hamiltonian of these states is traceless at every 𝐤\mathbf{k}, so the total filling is correct for any λ\lambda, but λ\lambda alone controls how the fermions are shared between the two sublattices. With λ=0\lambda=0 the total is right while the constraint on each site is violated; for UA31 at Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2 and J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2 the violation is |⟨nμ⟩−3/2|=0.33|\langle n_{\mu}\rangle-3/2|=0.33, and the energy is spuriously lowered by 0.11​J10.11\,J_{1}.

The second feature is the global gauge transformation τ1\tau^{1}. It maps χ3→−χ3\chi^{3}\to-\chi^{3}, λ→−λ\lambda\to-\lambda, and ζ→−ζ\zeta\to-\zeta, and hence maps the particle implementation exactly onto the hole implementation. The Nf=1N_{f}=1 and Nf=2N_{f}=2 phase diagrams are identical, with all second-neighbor hopping amplitudes reversed in sign. The same transformation applied to one sublattice only relates the paired Ansatz ZA3110 to UA31: the two describe the same state, with the constraint sectors exchanged on that sublattice.

The transformation τ1\tau^{1} also decides which constraint sectors are symmetric. For UA31 and UB31 the staggered onsite term is allowed only because the gauge parts of the sublattice-exchanging operations S4S_{4} and C¯3\bar{C}_{3} lie in the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} coset. These operations leave the staggered field invariant but reverse the uniform chemical potential that fixes the overall filling, so they map the sector (n0,n1)(n_{0},n_{1}) onto (3−n1,3−n0)(3-n_{1},3-n_{0}) (Appendix F). At Nf=1N_{f}=1 the symmetric realization of either Ansatz therefore has the two sublattices in opposite constraint sectors, (n0,n1)=(1,2)(n_{0},n_{1})=(1,2); for UA31 this is ZA3110 with χ1=0\chi_{1}=0 (uniform ζ=+1\zeta=+1 and singlet pairing on the first-neighbor bonds). A realization with ⟨ni⟩=1\langle n_{i}\rangle=1 on both sublattices is symmetric only if it is self-dual, i.e., if it coincides with the (1,1)(1,1) realization with reversed χ2\chi_{2} and λ\lambda; Sec. V.2 and Appendix F discuss when this holds. For UA01 and UB01, whose onsite term is uniform, the gauge parts of S4S_{4} and C¯3\bar{C}_{3} lie in U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), and only the uniform realization (1,1)(1,1) is symmetric.

The mixed-sector realizations must be included in the particle and hole phase diagrams alongside the uniform ones. We label the three implementations by the sublattice fillings Nf=(n0,n1)N_{f}=(n_{0},n_{1}): (3/2,3/2)(3/2,3/2), (1,1)≡(2,2)(1,1)\equiv(2,2), and (1,2)≡(2,1)(1,2)\equiv(2,1). In the mixed sector (1,2)(1,2) the particle representation is imposed on sublattice 00 and the hole representation on sublattice 11, ⟨Tr⁡[ψi​τ3​ψi†]⟩=±1\langle{\rm Tr}[\psi_{i}\tau^{3}\psi_{i}^{\dagger}]\rangle=\pm 1. The average filling is 3/23/2, as in the particle-hole-symmetric treatment, but every site has the integer filling of a spin-11 sector, as in the uniform sector. The staggered multiplier enforces n0−n1=−1n_{0}-n_{1}=-1 at every self-consistency step, and its contribution λ⁡(n0−n1)/2\lambda(n_{0}-n_{1})/2 per site is subtracted from the reported energies. A uniform multiplier, as in UA01 and UB01, couples only to the total density, which is already fixed, and cannot produce this imbalance; so these two Ansätze have no (1,2)(1,2) realization, in agreement with the symmetry argument. Figure 3 shows the energies of the three implementations.

V.1 Particle–hole symmetric constraint, Nf=(3/2,3/2)N_{f}=(3/2,3/2)

Figure 3(a) shows the energies. At this filling the constraint is invariant under the global transformation τ1\tau^{1}, which then acts as a gauge transformation. It maps (χ2,λ)→(−χ2,−λ)(\chi_{2},\lambda)\to(-\chi_{2},-\lambda) and leaves the first-neighbor amplitudes unchanged up to a sublattice sign in U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1). The point χ2=λ=0\chi_{2}=\lambda=0, where this element belongs to the IGG, is therefore always a self-consistent solution, and for all four hopping Ansätze it is the stable one at small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. There the second-neighbor amplitude is exactly zero, and the energies of UA01, UA31, and ZA3110 equal that of the parent state SA3, E/N=−0.9104​J1E/N=-0.9104\,J_{1}, while UB01 and UB31 equal SB1, E/N=−0.8111​J1E/N=-0.8111\,J_{1}.

This regime ends in one of two ways. In the two states with a staggered onsite term, (χ2,λ)(\chi_{2},\lambda) turns on continuously: at J2/J1=0.840J_{2}/J_{1}=0.840 in UA31 (equivalently ZA3110), whose nodal spectrum then becomes gapped, and at J2/J1≃0.62J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.62 in UB31. The two signs of (χ2,λ)(\chi_{2},\lambda) are related by τ1\tau^{1} and describe the same physical state, so this is not a symmetry breaking. The IGG is reduced from U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} to U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), the lattice symmetries and time reversal remain projectively realized, and the staggered λ\lambda keeps both sublattices at ⟨N^i⟩=3/2\langle\hat{N}_{i}\rangle=3/2. In the sense of the constraint, particle-hole symmetry is preserved throughout panel (a), whereas the constraints of panels (b) and (c) break it explicitly.

In UA01 and UB01, which have no staggered term, the first-neighbor amplitude instead collapses discontinuously, χ1→0\chi_{1}\to 0, at J2/J1≃0.74J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.74 (UB01) and 1.421.42 (UA01). The two FCC sublattices then decouple, and the energy becomes exactly linear in J2J_{2}, E/N=−6​χ22​J2E/N=-6\,\chi^{2}_{2}\,J_{2}, with a J2J_{2}-independent χ2\chi_{2} (0.42660.4266 for UB01, 0.32700.3270 for UA01). In UB31 the first-neighbor amplitude decreases continuously and vanishes at J2/J1≃1.0J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.0. Beyond it UB31 coincides with the decoupled UB01 state: once the sublattices decouple, the second-neighbor patterns of the two states on sublattice μ=1\mu=1 differ only by an overall sign, which does not matter at half filling of a single sublattice, and the staggered λ\lambda vanishes.

For 0.62≲J2/J1≲1.00.62\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1.0 the coupled UB31 state with (χ2,λ)≠0(\chi_{2},\lambda)\neq 0 lies below the decoupled state, by 0.006​J10.006\,J_{1} at J2/J1=0.85J_{2}/J_{1}=0.85 and 0.002​J10.002\,J_{1} at 0.90.9, and the difference vanishes at J2/J1≃1.0J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.0. The coupled state is gapped; the gap decreases from 0.94​J10.94\,J_{1} at J2/J1=0.8J_{2}/J_{1}=0.8 to 0.49​J10.49\,J_{1} at 0.90.9 and closes as χ1→0\chi_{1}\to 0. Among the computed states, the phase diagram is

0≤J2/J1≲0.82:\displaystyle 0\leq J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.82: SA3⁡(UA01=UA31),\displaystyle\quad\mathrm{SA3}\ (\text{UA01}=\text{UA31}), (60)
0.82≲J2/J1≲1.0:\displaystyle 0.82\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1.0: UB31 (coupled),\displaystyle\quad\text{UB31 (coupled)}, (61)
J2/J1≳1.0:\displaystyle J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 1.0: UB31=UB01 (decoupled),\displaystyle\quad\text{UB31}=\text{UB01 (decoupled)}, (62)

where SA3 is realized by UA01, UA31, and ZA3110 alike.

V.2 Uniform particle and hole constraints, Nf=(1,1)≡(2,2)N_{f}=(1,1)\equiv(2,2)

Figure 3(b) shows the (1,1)(1,1) energies; the (2,2)(2,2) diagram is identical. In this sector the constraint breaks particle-hole symmetry explicitly for all four states. The breaking of S4S_{4} and C¯3\bar{C}_{3} discussed below has a different origin: the gauge part τ1\tau^{1} of these operations maps the (1,1)(1,1) sector onto (2,2)(2,2), so a (1,1)(1,1) realization of UA31 or UB31 is symmetric only if it is self-dual (Appendix F).

At J2=0J_{2}=0 the hopping states have E/N=−0.6458​J1E/N=-0.6458\,J_{1} (SA3) and −0.6681​J1-0.6681\,J_{1} (SB1). How they evolve with J2J_{2} follows from an identity of the diamond lattice, Γ2​(𝐤)=|g1​(𝐤)|2−4\Gamma_{2}(\mathbf{k})=|g_{1}(\mathbf{k})|^{2}-4, with g1=∑1​N​Nei​𝐤⋅𝜹g_{1}=\sum_{\rm 1NN}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}} and Γ2=∑2​N​Nei​𝐤⋅𝐝\Gamma_{2}=\sum_{\rm 2NN}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{d}}. For UA01 both the first- and second-neighbor dispersions depend on 𝐤\mathbf{k} only through |g1||g_{1}|. The set of occupied states, and hence χ1\chi_{1} and χ2\chi_{2}, do not change with J2J_{2} until the band ordering changes, and between such rearrangements the energy is exactly linear in J2J_{2} (E/N=−0.6459−0.104​J2E/N=-0.6459-0.104\,J_{2} for UA01 up to J2/J1=1.1J_{2}/J_{1}=1.1, then −0.8205-0.8205 at 1.21.2 with a much larger χ2\chi_{2}). Among the symmetric states of this sector, UB01 is lowest up to J2/J1≃1.37J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.37 and UA01 above, in a form with a nearly vanishing first-neighbor amplitude (E/N=−1.3675​J1E/N=-1.3675\,J_{1} at J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2).

The (1,1)(1,1) realizations of UA31 and UB31 converge to the nearest-neighbor states SA3 and SB1 (χ2=0\chi_{2}=0) for J2/J1≲1.1J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1.1. Above this, UB31 becomes the decoupled class-B state, which is self-dual and hence symmetric. UA31 instead develops χ2≠0\chi_{2}\neq 0 and a staggered λ\lambda, and it breaks the sublattice-exchanging operations S4S_{4} and C¯3\bar{C}_{3}. With χ1≃0\chi_{1}\simeq 0 its two FCC sublattices decouple and carry second-neighbor hopping of opposite sign at filling 1/31/3. Because the FCC lattice is not bipartite, these two sublattice states are physically different: their second-neighbor bond energies differ by about 25%25\%, although S4S_{4} maps one sublattice onto the other. Both states lie above UA01 and UB01 throughout.

V.3 Mixed constraint, Nf=(1,2)N_{f}=(1,2)

Figure 3(c) shows the energies of the symmetric mixed-sector realizations of UA31 and UB31. ZA3110 ≡\equiv UA31(1,2)\,(1,2) has E/N=−0.8355​J1E/N=-0.8355\,J_{1} at J2=0J_{2}=0 and is the lowest computed state up to J2/J1≃0.67J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.67. The mixed-sector UB31 state starts higher, at −0.7616​J1-0.7616\,J_{1}, but gains energy faster with J2J_{2}. It is the lowest computed state above J2/J1≃0.67J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.67. Unlike the class-B states at Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2, it keeps a sizable first-neighbor amplitude (χ1=0.48\chi_{1}=0.48 at J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2) and is gapped throughout, with a spinon gap that grows from 1.81​J11.81\,J_{1} at J2/J1=0.7J_{2}/J_{1}=0.7 to 2.45​J12.45\,J_{1} at J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2. ZA3110 is also gapped, with a largest gap 2​Emin=2.16​J12E_{\min}=2.16\,J_{1} at J2/J1≃1.1J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.1.

The mixed sector lies below the uniform one at every coupling [dotted line in Fig. 3(c)]. Both sectors give every site the integer filling of a spin-11 sector, so the lowest computed state in the particle and hole representations is ZA3110 ≡\equiv UA31(1,2)\,(1,2) for J2/J1≲0.674J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.674 and the mixed-sector UB31 state above.

V.4 The ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz ZA3110

When all three amplitudes of ZA3110 are left free, the self-consistent first-neighbor hopping χ1\chi_{1} vanishes at every point we examined, for all three constraints. The surviving state, u1=i​Δ1​τ1u_{1}=i\Delta_{1}\tau^{1}, u2=χ2​τ3u_{2}=\chi_{2}\tau^{3} has an enlarged IGG U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), and is thus a U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state written in a pairing gauge rather than a genuine ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state at the saddle point. This is a gauge image of UA31 described above in a modified constraint sector discussed in the following.

The connection is made by the gauge transformation W=τ0W=\tau^{0} on one sublattice and W=ei​π2​τ3​τ1W=e^{i\frac{\pi}{2}\tau^{3}}\tau^{1} on the other. It maps i​Δ1​τ1i\Delta_{1}\tau^{1} onto the hopping Δ1​τ3\Delta_{1}\tau^{3}, so that Δ1\Delta_{1} becomes the first-neighbor hopping of UA31; it turns the uniform χ2\chi_{2} and λ\lambda into the staggered ±χ2\pm\chi_{2} and ±λ\pm\lambda; and, because WW contains τ1\tau^{1}, it sends Nf→3−NfN_{f}\to 3-N_{f} on the rotated sublattice. Hence ZA3110 at Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2 is UA31 at (3/2,3/2)(3/2,3/2), contained in Fig. 3(a), and ZA3110 at Nf=1N_{f}=1 or 22 is UA31 at (1,2)(1,2) or (2,1)(2,1), contained in Fig. 3(c). Up to second neighbors the classification contains no realized ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} state: the algebraic ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} PSG ZA3110 yields a U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state at the saddle point, adds no saddle point beyond the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) hopping states, and is not drawn separately. This is specific to S>1/2S>1/2: for S=1/2S=1/2 the particle and hole representations coincide, and the analogous rotation does not change the constraint sector.

V.5 Particle-hole-averaged representation

Since the phase diagram depends on how the constraint is implemented, one may ask whether there is a representation in which any generic U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge transformation does not change the constraint sector at all. For integer spin, Liu, Zhou, and Ng [25] constructed one by averaging the partition function over the particle and hole constraints on every site, ∏i12​[δ⁡(N^i−1)+δ⁡(N^i−2​S)]\prod_{i}\tfrac{1}{2}[\delta(\hat{N}_{i}-1)+\delta(\hat{N}_{i}-2S)]. This representation of the spin model is exact, and the constraint enters the Lagrangian through the weight cosh⁡[(2​S−1)​λ~i/2]\cosh[(2S-1)\tilde{\lambda}_{i}/2] of the multiplier λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i}. The weight is even under λ~i→−λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\to-\tilde{\lambda}_{i}, which is the action of the τ1∈ℤ2\tau^{1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{2} coset of U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}, so the Lagrangian is invariant under the full internal group U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The constraint then places no restriction on the PSG: λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} is an onsite field like any other, uniform for UA01 and UB01 and staggered for UA31 and UB31, and every saddle point is symmetric. The local rotation that maps ZA3110 onto UA31 leaves the averaged constraint invariant, so these two Ansätze again have the same saddle points.

At the saddle point the mean-field Hamiltonian acquires the terms ∑i[λ~i​(N^i−2​S+12)−β−1​ln⁡cosh⁡β⁡(2​S−1)​λ~i2]\sum_{i}[\tilde{\lambda}_{i}(\hat{N}_{i}-\tfrac{2S+1}{2})-\beta^{-1}\ln\cosh\tfrac{\beta(2S-1)\tilde{\lambda}_{i}}{2}], and the constraint becomes

⟨N^i⟩−2​S+12=2​S−12​tanh⁡β⁡(2​S−1)​λ~i2,\langle\hat{N}_{i}\rangle-\frac{2S+1}{2}=\frac{2S-1}{2}\tanh\frac{\beta(2S-1)\tilde{\lambda}_{i}}{2}, (63)

where β\beta is the imaginary-time interval on which the average over the two constraints is inserted. Inserting it on every time slice and taking the continuum limit gives β→0\beta\to 0; a single insertion at temperature TT gives β=1/T\beta=1/T. The unscaled form written in Ref. [25] corresponds to β=1/J\beta=1/J. For fixed amplitudes, Eq. (63) is the maximum of a concave function of λ~i\tilde{\lambda}_{i} and has a unique solution. For β→0\beta\to 0 it reduces to ⟨N^i⟩=(2​S+1)/2\langle\hat{N}_{i}\rangle=(2S+1)/2, the particle-hole-symmetric implementation of Fig. 3(a). For β→∞\beta\to\infty it relaxes the constraint to the inequality 1≤⟨N^i⟩≤2​S1\leq\langle\hat{N}_{i}\rangle\leq 2S, with λ~i=0\tilde{\lambda}_{i}=0 whenever the inequality holds; the exact sectors (1,1)(1,1) and (1,2)(1,2) are then saddle points only if the band structure itself produces integer occupations.

Figure 4 shows the zero-temperature saddle points of a single insertion, β→∞\beta\to\infty; the opposite limit, β→0\beta\to 0, is Fig. 3(a). States with particle-hole-symmetric spectra are the same in both limits: SA3, SB1, and the decoupled class-B state. The limits differ only where the single-particle spectrum is not particle-hole symmetric, so that without the multiplier the occupations move away from 3/23/2. UA31 and UB31 then develop occupations with ⟨N^0⟩+⟨N^1⟩=3\langle\hat{N}_{0}\rangle+\langle\hat{N}_{1}\rangle=3, and the decoupled form of UA01 develops uniform occupations ⟨N^0⟩=⟨N^1⟩≠3/2\langle\hat{N}_{0}\rangle=\langle\hat{N}_{1}\rangle\neq 3/2. In UB31, particle-hole symmetry in the sense ⟨N^i⟩≠3/2\langle\hat{N}_{i}\rangle\neq 3/2 is broken from J2/J1≃0.25J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.25; for β→0\beta\to 0 it is never broken, and (χ2,λ)(\chi_{2},\lambda) sets in only at 0.620.62. The occupations move towards the exact sectors, reaching (⟨N^0⟩,⟨N^1⟩)=(1.15,1.85)(\langle\hat{N}_{0}\rangle,\langle\hat{N}_{1}\rangle)=(1.15,1.85) for UB31 at J2/J1=0.6J_{2}/J_{1}=0.6 and (1.17,1.83)(1.17,1.83) for UA31 at J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2. The averaged representation thus pushes the staggered Ansätze towards the mixed sector (1,2)(1,2), which is lowest in Fig. 3(c).

The lowest states come in the same order as in Fig. 3(a): SA3, then a state with (χ2,λ)≠0(\chi_{2},\lambda)\neq 0, then the decoupled class-B state. The middle window is wider, with UA31 lowest for 0.55≲J2/J1≲0.740.55\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.74 and UB31 up to J2/J1≃1.1J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.1, compared with UB31 alone for 0.82≲J2/J1≲1.00.82\lesssim J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 1.0 when β→0\beta\to 0. The unscaled form of Ref. [25], β=1/J1\beta=1/J_{1}, lies between the two limits; its first boundary is at J2/J1≃0.79J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.79. Because the averaged representation enforces the constraint only on average, its energies lie below those of the exact sectors, as in the one-dimensional case [25]. It gives a manifestly symmetric mean-field framework, but for the spin model the relevant comparison is between the exact sectors of Secs. V.2 and V.3.

V.6 Comparison with previous studies and experiment

The pseudofermion functional renormalization group study of Ref. [7] found that for S≤1S\leq 1 the J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} diamond antiferromagnet does not order in the spiral regime J2/J1>1/8J_{2}/J_{1}>1/8 and forms a quantum spiral spin liquid, whereas for S≥3/2S\geq 3/2 it orders. In our particle-hole-symmetric phase diagram, the region J2/J1≳0.8J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 0.8 of that regime belongs to the class-B states, which for J2/J1≳1.0J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 1.0 reduce at the saddle point to decoupled FCC sublattices with the class-B second-neighbor hopping pattern. In the particle and hole representations the same region belongs to the mixed-sector UB31 state. This state is gapped, with a spinon gap of about 2​J12\,J_{1}, and so is ZA3110 at smaller J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}. The decoupled class-B state of the particle-hole-symmetric treatment is instead gapless: its bands touch at 𝐤=(π/2,π/2,π/2)\mathbf{k}=(\pi/2,\pi/2,\pi/2) and the equivalent points of the reduced zone of the 8-site cell, and the gap of the coupled UB31 state that precedes it (0.49​J10.49\,J_{1} at J2/J1=0.9J_{2}/J_{1}=0.9) closes as χ1→0\chi_{1}\to 0.

The spin-11 diamond-lattice material NiRh2O4 shows no magnetic order and has gapped magnetic excitations in inelastic neutron scattering [9]. Gapped spinons are a feature of the candidate states of the particle and hole representations in this regime, but the comparison can only be qualitative. The neutron gap belongs to a physical spin excitation; the measured sample was substoichiometric and tetragonally distorted, with a sizable single-ion anisotropy [9, 7]; and a quantitative comparison requires projection and gauge fluctuations beyond the present saddle-point treatment.

VI General filling constraint on gapped U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states

Why the uniform sector is gapless while the mixed sector is gapped follows from a counting argument that holds for any spin SS and any lattice. A U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) Ansatz conserves the spinon number in a suitable gauge, and its 2​S+12S+1 flavors occupy identical bands. Let the unit cell contain n0n_{0} sites, npn_{p} of them in the particle sector (Ni=1N_{i}=1) and nhn_{h} in the hole sector (Ni=2​SN_{i}=2S); these are the only two sectors that carry spin SS. Let the projective translations enlarge the unit cell of the gauge-fixed Ansatz by a factor qq. For the time-reversal-symmetric Ansätze considered here the translation phases are ±1\pm 1, and qq is a power of two (q=1q=1 for class A and q=4q=4 for class B). The number of occupied states per flavor and enlarged unit cell is then

F=q​np+2​S​nh2​S+1.F=q\,\frac{n_{p}+2S\,n_{h}}{2S+1}. (64)

A gapped mean-field state needs an integer number of filled bands, F∈ℤF\in\mathbb{Z}. Otherwise a band is partially filled with a fractional Luttinger volume, and the state has a spinon Fermi surface. The condition is necessary but not sufficient, as the nodal SA3 state at F=1F=1 shows.

In the uniform sectors F=q​n0/(2​S+1)F=qn_{0}/(2S+1) or q​n0​ 2​S/(2​S+1)qn_{0}\,2S/(2S+1). Since 2​S2S and 2​S+12S+1 are coprime, a gap requires (2​S+1)|q​n0(2S+1)\mid qn_{0}, which for integer SS and time-reversal-symmetric Ansätze means (2​S+1)|n0(2S+1)\mid n_{0}. For S=1S=1 on the diamond lattice (n0=2n_{0}=2) the particle sector has F=2/3F=2/3 for the class-A and F=8/3F=8/3 for the class-B Ansätze. Every symmetric U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state of the uniform sectors (1,1)(1,1) and (2,2)(2,2) therefore has a spinon Fermi surface, as we find numerically. In the mixed sector, 2​S≡−1(mod2​S+1)2S\equiv-1\pmod{2S+1} gives F∈ℤF\in\mathbb{Z} whenever (2​S+1)|q⁡(np−nh)(2S+1)\mid q(n_{p}-n_{h}), in particular for every SS when the two sublattices of a bipartite lattice are in opposite sectors, np=nhn_{p}=n_{h}. Paired (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}) states do not conserve the spinon number and are not constrained.

A gapped symmetric mean-field state of an integer-spin magnet with (2​S+1)∤n0(2S+1)\nmid n_{0} must therefore be paired, or gauge equivalent to a mixed-sector U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state, as ZA3110 is. This is the free-parton analog of the flux-insertion argument for fermions at fractional filling [36]. It does not constrain the spin model itself: the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis theorem [22, 16] restricts only the spin per unit cell, which is an integer here, and beyond mean field the spinon number is a gauge charge.

The same counting decides the fate of the nodal structure inherited from the spin-1/21/2 classification. The nodal manifold of the spin-1/21/2 SA3 state, protected by the projective screw and rotoinversion symmetries [10], is also present in the corresponding spin-11 hopping Ansatz. Whether it lies at the Fermi level depends on how the constraint is implemented. In the hopping form of these states the spinon filling is 1/31/3 in the particle representation and 2/32/3 in the hole representation, and the nodal manifold is replaced by a Fermi surface. It lies at the Fermi energy only at the particle-hole-symmetric saddle point, where the filling is 1/21/2. The mixed-sector states that are lowest in the particle and hole representations, ZA3110 and UB31, are fully gapped.

VII Static structure factor

Figures 5 and 6 show the equal-time structure factors of the lowest computed states. In every regime the intensity is organized around the Néel wave vector H=(4​π,0,0)\mathrm{H}=(4\pi,0,0). Scanning J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1} gives four qualitatively different forms [Fig. 6(e,f)], and within each regime S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) changes continuously. At Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2, SA3 has a single maximum at H, elongated along ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle. The class-B states have S⁡(H)→0S(\mathrm{H})\to 0 and a shell of maxima on the boundary of the first zone around H, strongest at the X points and with deep minima along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle (25%25\% modulation); the coupled UB31 state differs from the decoupled one only by a small S⁡(H)S(\mathrm{H}), which vanishes continuously. At Nf=1,2N_{f}=1,2, ZA3110 also has its maximum at H, but with the opposite anisotropy, flattened along ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle. The mixed-sector UB31 state has a closed shell of maxima inside the zone on top of a broad maximum at H, with minima along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle whose depth grows from 0.2%0.2\% at J2/J1=0.7J_{2}/J_{1}=0.7 to 5%5\% at J2/J1=2J_{2}/J_{1}=2.

Figure 7 compares these results with the classical Luttinger-Tisza (LT) analysis [4]. In the true-position (atomic) gauge the LT matrix has eigenvalues ω±​(𝐪)=J2​(|g1​(𝐪)|2−4)±J1​|g1​(𝐪)|\omega_{\pm}(\mathbf{q})=J_{2}(|g_{1}(\mathbf{q})|^{2}-4)\pm J_{1}|g_{1}(\mathbf{q})|. For J2/J1>1/8J_{2}/J_{1}>1/8 the minima form the spiral surface |g1​(𝐪)|=J1/2​J2|g_{1}(\mathbf{q})|=J_{1}/2J_{2}. In this gauge the surface is centered at H; it is closed for J2/J1<1/4J_{2}/J_{1}<1/4 and open along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle above. In the structure factor the lower LT mode carries the weight w⁡(𝐪)=1−cos⁡arg⁡g1​(𝐪)w(\mathbf{q})=1-\cos\arg g_{1}(\mathbf{q}), which equals 22 at H and lies between 11 and 22 on the surface within the first zone around H.

Classically, spiral-surface correlations set in at J2/J1=1/8J_{2}/J_{1}=1/8. The lowest mean-field states, by contrast, keep their maximum at H up to J2/J1=0.82J_{2}/J_{1}=0.82 (Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2) and 0.6740.674 (Nf=1,2N_{f}=1,2) [Fig. 7(e)]. Above these values the shells of both class-B states have the topology of the open classical surface, with minima along ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle. The shell of the Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2 states lies close to the classical surface (within 10%10\% along [100][100] and 3%3\% along [110][110]) and to the zone boundary, while that of the mixed-sector UB31 state lies well inside it, at 0.710.71–0.790.79 of the classical radius for J2/J1≥1J_{2}/J_{1}\geq 1. The directions of largest intensity are X for Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2, and ⟨110⟩\langle 110\rangle and ⟨100⟩\langle 100\rangle (nearly degenerate) for the mixed-sector state. These can be compared with the classical thermal order-by-disorder selection for J2/J1>2/3J_{2}/J_{1}>2/3, around the (q,0,0)(q,0,0) directions [4]. The modulation along the mean-field shells is weak, however, so the intensity is spread over a surface rather than concentrated at isolated wave vectors, as in the functional renormalization group study of Ref. [7].

VIII Summary and outlook

We have extended the projective symmetry group classification, which has underpinned the theory of spin-1/21/2 quantum spin liquids for twenty-five years, to fermionic partons of arbitrary spin SS. Higher-spin candidate materials and synthetic magnets now have a systematic list of the symmetric spin liquids they can host. For S>1/2S\!>\!1/2 the particle and hole representations are no longer equivalent, and the internal redundancy of the representation depends on whether the spin is integer or half-odd-integer. This leads to different invariant gauge groups. For integer spin they include U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} and ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and the latter has no analog in the spin-1/21/2 classification. Integer-spin quantum spin liquids can realize projective symmetries in ways that do not occur for spin 1/21/2.

For the spin-11 diamond lattice with amplitudes on first- and second-neighbor bonds, the classification gives ten fully symmetric Ansätze: two with IGG U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2}, five with U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1), two with ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2}, and one with ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}. The hopping-only states have the link structure of the spin-1/21/2 classification but a different gauge structure, because the internal symmetry group is different. The paired states differ more: the spin-11 singlet pairing field is odd under site interchange, unlike the even singlet pairing of spin-1/21/2 Abrikosov fermions, and this restricts the allowed paired Ansätze and changes the pattern of ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants.

We then studied the antiferromagnetic J1J_{1}–J2J_{2} Heisenberg model with these Ansätze, including the symmetry-allowed staggered onsite terms of UA31 and UB31. In the particle-hole-symmetric treatment (Nf=3/2N_{f}=3/2) the second-neighbor amplitudes of all hopping states vanish identically at small J2/J1J_{2}/J_{1}, and the lowest computed state is the U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} state SA3 up to J2/J1≃0.82J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 0.82. The class-B state UB31 takes over beyond this point. It is first gapped, with nonzero second-neighbor and staggered onsite amplitudes and a small first-neighbor amplitude. For J2/J1≳1.0J_{2}/J_{1}\gtrsim 1.0 the first-neighbor amplitude vanishes and the two FCC sublattices decouple, which leaves a gapless state of two independent FCC lattices with second-neighbor hopping, in which UB01 and UB31 are degenerate. This regime overlaps with the nonmagnetic regime found in earlier studies of the spin-11 diamond antiferromagnet.

The particle and hole representations, Nf=1N_{f}=1 and Nf=2N_{f}=2, are exact images of each other under the global ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge transformation and give identical phase diagrams. For UA31 and UB31 at fixed filling, the gauge parts of S4S_{4} and C¯3\bar{C}_{3} exchange the particle and hole representations between the sublattices. Their symmetric realizations therefore have the two sublattices in opposite constraint sectors. A uniform-sector realization is symmetric only if it is self-dual, as the decoupled class-B state is; otherwise, as for UA31 with χ2≠0\chi_{2}\neq 0, it breaks the sublattice-exchange symmetry (Appendix F). UA01 and UB01 are symmetric only in the uniform sector, where the lowest state is UB01 up to J2/J1≃1.37J_{2}/J_{1}\simeq 1.37 and UA01 above. The mixed sector lies lower at every coupling. A counting argument explains why the uniform-sector states are gapless: for integer spin, a symmetric U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state in the uniform sector can be gapped only if the number of sites per unit cell is a multiple of 2​S+12S+1, whereas mixed-sector states on a bipartite lattice and paired states are not restricted. Among the symmetric realizations we computed, the lowest state is the paired Ansatz ZA3110 at its self-consistent point χ1=0\chi_{1}=0, which is the mixed-sector realization of UA31, for J2/J1≲0.67J_{2}/J_{1}\lesssim 0.67, and the mixed-sector realization of UB31 above. Both are gapped, and the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansatz adds no saddle point beyond the U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) hopping states. In the particle-hole-averaged representation of Ref. [25], where the internal ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} leaves the constraint invariant and every saddle point is symmetric, the lowest states come in the same order as in the particle-hole-symmetric treatment; the window with (χ2,λ)≠0(\chi_{2},\lambda)\neq 0 widens, and its occupations move towards the mixed sector. The phase diagram, and properties of the candidate states such as whether nodal structures lie at the Fermi level, thus depend on how the spin-11 constraint is implemented.

This dependence is the main limitation of the saddle-point analysis. The particle-hole-symmetric treatment keeps the symmetry between the two representations, but it implements neither physical constraint exactly. The particle and hole representations impose the correct integer fillings at mean-field level, but they treat two inequivalent embeddings of the spin-11 Hilbert space separately. A natural next step is to study the classified Ansätze with variational Monte Carlo, where the particle and hole constraints can be imposed exactly by projection. This would allow a direct comparison between the constraint representations and a stronger test of the candidate spin liquids identified here.

Restricting the classification to second-neighbor amplitudes also leaves some parent states without paired descendants. Within this restriction, the class-B U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) states and the ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} states do not all have ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendants. Extending the construction to third-neighbor bonds gives four further ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} Ansätze, listed in the last four rows of Table 4 (Appendix D), but UB01 still has no ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} descendant. The descendant structure of integer-spin PSGs thus appears to be more restrictive than for spin 1/21/2, and longer-range amplitudes may be needed to reveal the full set of nearby paired spin liquids.

The classification also gives a systematic way into materials and models that have so far been treated case by case. Nothing in the construction is specific to the diamond lattice. It applies to any lattice and any spin, and the spin-1/21/2 classifications already available for the kagome [27], triangular [28], and pyrochlore [23] lattices supply the link structure on which the integer-spin gauge structure can be built. Natural next targets are the spin-11 pyrochlore NaCaNi2F7, whose neutron spectra show a continuum of quantum fluctuations [37], and the langbeinite K2Ni2(SO4)3, in which a field-induced spin-liquid regime on two coupled trillium lattices has been reported [45, 14]. The counting rule of Sec. VI already constrains both. The pyrochlore lattice has four sites per primitive cell and K2Ni2(SO4)3 has eight Ni2+ ions per cubic cell; neither is a multiple of 2​S+1=32S+1=3, so every time-reversal-symmetric spin-11 U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) state in a uniform constraint sector has a spinon Fermi surface, and a gapped spin liquid in these materials must be paired or of mixed-sector type. For the spin-3/23/2 and spin-5/25/2 spinels CoAl2O4 and MnSc2S4 [30, 13], the half-odd-integer hierarchy applies instead, and the same framework can address whether the spiral spin-liquid regime of the classical model [4] survives as a quantum spin liquid. For spin-11 Rydberg arrays [24, 33], the classified Ansätze give candidate states to compare with quantum simulations. Together with projected wave functions and the structure factors computed from them, the spin-SS PSG can be used to identify fractionalized phases in higher-spin magnets generally.

𝒲𝒪​(μ)\displaystyle\mathcal{W}_{\mathcal{O}}(\mu) ∈U⁡(1)⋊ℤ2\displaystyle\in\mathrm{U}(1)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_{2} (73)
